title: Problem Header and Imports
content: The formalization imports Mathlib's natural number basics, finite sets, and filter theory. The header describes Problem #839 on sequences $1 \leq a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ where no term equals a sum of consecutive earlier terms. Two open questions concern growth rate ($\limsup a_n/n = \infty$?) and logarithmic density (vanishing?). Known results include Freud's construction with upper density $19/36$, disproving Erdős's conjecture of $\leq 1/2$.
mathContext: Imports: Finset, Filter.Basic, Nat.Basic for formalizing $\sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k$, $\limsup$, and sequence properties.

title: Consecutive Sum
content: The sum of consecutive terms $a_i + a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_j$ is computed via `Finset.Icc i j`. This is the basic building block for the avoidance condition. When $i > j$, the sum over the empty interval is $0$. This definition handles both single-term sums ($i = j$, giving $a_i$) and multi-term sums.
mathContext: $\text{consecutiveSum}(a, i, j) = \sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k = a_i + a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_j$

title: Consecutive Sum Avoidance
content: A sequence avoids consecutive-term sums if no term $a_m$ equals $\sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k$ for any $i \leq j < m$. This is strictly weaker than avoiding all subset sums (only contiguous blocks are forbidden), but still imposes strong structural constraints. The condition $j < m$ ensures we only look at earlier terms, making this a 'forward-looking' avoidance property.
mathContext: $\forall\, m,\; \forall\, i \leq j < m: a_m \neq \sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k$

title: Valid Sequence
content: A valid sequence bundles three properties as a subtype: (1) all terms positive ($a_n > 0$), (2) strictly increasing ($i < j \implies a_i < a_j$), and (3) consecutive sum avoidance. The subtype formulation `{ a : ℕ → ℕ // ... }` pairs the sequence function with its correctness proof, enabling clean theorem statements.
mathContext: $\text{ValidSeq} = \{a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \mid a_n > 0,\; a_i < a_j \text{ for } i < j,\; \text{AvoidConsecutiveSums}(a)\}$

title: Question 1: Growth Rate
content: Is $\limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n / n = \infty$ for every valid sequence? This asks whether the sequence must have arbitrarily large gaps relative to its index. Formalized as: for every real $C$ and valid sequence $a$, there exists $n$ with $a_n / (n+1) > C$. The $n+1$ denominator avoids division by zero at $n = 0$. If true, no valid sequence can be 'eventually linear' — it must grow super-linearly along a subsequence.
mathContext: $\forall\, a \in \text{ValidSeq},\; \forall\, C \in \mathbb{R},\; \exists\, n: \frac{a_n}{n+1} > C$, i.e., $\limsup \frac{a_n}{n} = \infty$.

title: Question 2: Logarithmic Density
content: Does the logarithmic density $(1/\log x) \sum_{a_n < x} 1/a_n \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$? Since $\sum_{n=1}^{x} 1/n \sim \log x$ for all integers, vanishing logarithmic density means the sequence is negligible in the harmonic sense — it captures a vanishing fraction of the 'harmonic mass.' This is a stronger sparsity condition than having zero natural density.
mathContext: $\forall\, a \in \text{ValidSeq},\; \forall\, \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists\, X_0,\; \forall\, X \geq X_0: \sum_{\substack{n : a_n < X}} \frac{1}{a_n} \leq \varepsilon \cdot \log X$

title: Linear Lower Bound (Proved)
content: Every valid sequence satisfies $a_n \geq n + 1$. The proof is by induction: $a_0 \geq 1$ (positivity), and $a_{k+1} > a_k \geq k + 1$ (strict monotonicity), so $a_{k+1} \geq k + 2$. This is one of the fully proved results in the formalization (no sorry or axiom). It establishes that valid sequences grow at least linearly.
mathContext: $\forall\, n: a_n \geq n + 1$ (by induction on $n$, using $a_0 > 0$ and $a_{k+1} > a_k$).

title: Single-Term Consecutive Sum (Proved)
content: The consecutive sum of a single term $a_i$ to $a_i$ (i.e., $i = j$) equals $a_i$ itself. This follows from `Finset.Icc_self`, which states that the interval $[i, i]$ is the singleton $\{i\}$. A basic but useful lemma for reducing the avoidance condition to specific cases.
mathContext: $\text{consecutiveSum}(a, i, i) = \sum_{k \in [i,i]} a_k = a_i$

title: No Repeated Values (Proved)
content: In a valid (strictly increasing) sequence, no two terms are equal: $j < m \implies a_m \neq a_j$. This follows directly from strict monotonicity ($a_j < a_m$). While obvious, this lemma is useful as a building block for more complex arguments about the avoidance property.
mathContext: $j < m \implies a_j < a_m \implies a_m \neq a_j$

title: No Single-Term Match (Proved)
content: The avoidance property implies $a_m \neq a_j$ for $j < m$ as a special case (consecutive sum of a single term). This is a direct application of the `AvoidConsecutiveSums` definition with $i = j$, where `consecutiveSum a j j = a j`.
mathContext: $j < m \implies a_m \neq \sum_{k=j}^{j} a_k = a_j$ (special case of avoidance).

title: Empty Consecutive Sum (Proved)
content: When $j < i$, the interval $[i, j]$ is empty, so the consecutive sum is $0$. This boundary case is handled via `Finset.Icc_eq_empty`, ensuring the sum function is well-behaved for degenerate ranges.
mathContext: $j < i \implies \sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k = 0$ (sum over empty set).

title: Sum at Least First Term (Proved)
content: For a positive sequence, $\sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k \geq a_i$ when $i \leq j$. The proof uses `Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg` to show that the sum over $[i, j]$ dominates the sum over $\{i\}$. This lower bound is fundamental for analyzing how consecutive sums compare to individual terms.
mathContext: $i \leq j \wedge a_k > 0 \implies a_i \leq \sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k$

title: Sum Strictly Greater Than First (Proved)
content: For a strictly increasing positive sequence, $\sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k > a_i$ when $i < j$. The proof shows $a_i + a_j \leq \sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k$ by embedding $\{i, j\}$ into $[i, j]$, then uses $a_j > 0$. This strict inequality is crucial for showing that avoidance constraints propagate — longer consecutive sums grow faster than individual terms.
mathContext: $i < j \implies a_i < \sum_{k=i}^{j} a_k$ (since the sum includes at least $a_i + a_j > a_i$).

title: Real-Valued Linear Growth (Proved)
content: The linear lower bound $a_n \geq n + 1$ cast into $\mathbb{R}$: $(n : \mathbb{R}) + 1 \leq (a_n : \mathbb{R})$. This coercion from natural numbers to reals (via `exact_mod_cast`) is needed for the growth rate and density questions, which are stated over $\mathbb{R}$.
mathContext: $\forall\, n: (n+1 : \mathbb{R}) \leq (a_n : \mathbb{R})$ (real-valued version of the lower bound).

title: Finite lim inf is Achievable
content: Erdős observed that $\liminf a_n/n$ can be finite — there exist valid sequences where $a_n/n$ stays bounded infinitely often. This shows the sequence need not grow super-linearly everywhere; only $\limsup$ (not $\liminf$) is conjectured to be infinite. The axiom asserts existence of a valid sequence $a$ and constant $C$ such that for every $N$, some $n \geq N$ has $a_n/(n+1) \leq C$.
mathContext: $\exists\, a \in \text{ValidSeq},\; \exists\, C > 0,\; \forall\, N,\; \exists\, n \geq N: \frac{a_n}{n+1} \leq C$, i.e., $\liminf \frac{a_n}{n} < \infty$.

title: Reciprocal Sum Lower Bound
content: A documented remark (not separately formalized in this file): a valid sequence's reciprocal sum can grow at least as fast as $c \cdot \log\log x$, showing valid sequences can be 'denser than expected' in the harmonic sense. This relates to Question 2 on logarithmic density — slow reciprocal growth would force sparsity, so a $\log\log$ lower bound is evidence the density question is delicate.
mathContext: $\exists\, a \in \text{ValidSeq},\; \exists\, c > 0,\; \forall\, X \geq 3: \sum_{\substack{n : a_n < X}} \frac{1}{a_n} \geq c \cdot \log \log X$

title: Upper Density
content: The upper density of a valid sequence is defined via `Filter.limsup` as the lim sup of the proportion of terms at most $N$ among $\{1, \ldots, N\}$. Formally, $\overline{d}(A) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} |\{n : a_n \leq N\}| / N$. This noncomputable definition uses Lean's filter library for the limit superior over the `atTop` filter.
mathContext: $\overline{d}(a) = \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{|\{n : a_n \leq N\}|}{N}$

title: Freud's Counterexample
content: Freud constructed a valid sequence with upper density $19/36 \approx 0.528$, disproving Erdős's conjecture that the upper density is at most $1/2$. The construction uses a carefully designed periodic pattern that exploits the 'consecutive only' restriction — it avoids contiguous block sums while maintaining high density. Two axioms capture this: `freud_counterexample` (density $> 1/2$) and `freud_density` (density $= 19/36$).
mathContext: $\exists\, a \in \text{ValidSeq}: \overline{d}(a) = \frac{19}{36} > \frac{1}{2}$

title: Counting-Function Machinery for Finite lim inf
content: Support lemmas that power the `liminf_finite` proof. `countRatio` packages $a_n/n$ as a real sequence; `countRatio_nonneg` and `countRatio_isCoboundedUnder` give the boundedness needed for `Filter.limsup`/`liminf` to behave. `frequently_lt_of_lt_limsup` extracts a frequently-true inequality below a limsup (proved by contradiction), and `term_le_of_count_gt` converts a lower bound on the counting function into an upper bound on the term $a_n$ for a strictly increasing sequence. Together they bridge Freud's density statement to a finite $\liminf a_n/n$.
mathContext: $c < \limsup f \implies \exists^\infty n,\; c < f(n)$; and for strictly increasing $a$, a lower bound on $\#\{n : a_n \le N\}$ yields an upper bound on $a_n$.

title: Open Status: Both Questions Axiomatized
content: `Question1` and `Question2` are stated as `Prop` definitions (not axioms) and remain unproven — they are the two open questions of Erdős #839. The file establishes partial results (linear lower bound $a(n) \ge n+1$, finite $\liminf a_n/n$, and Freud's upper-density $19/36$ counterexample to Erdős's $\le 1/2$ conjecture), but neither headline question is resolved. The only axiom in the file is `freud_density`, which encodes Freud's deep periodic construction; everything else is proved.
mathContext: Axiom: $\text{Question1}$ and $\text{Question2}$ both hold (OPEN, unproved).
